## Fable [architect] [ok]

`claude --print --output-format text --permission-mode dontAsk --tools '' --strict-mcp-config --disable-slash-commands --safe-mode --append-system-prompt <read-only-review>  (prompt via stdin)`

Overall this is a well-layered change — tokenizer in `HyperGitCore` with colors in the app layer, checks model with roll-up logic in core and badge colors in the app — and the test coverage for the core logic is genuinely good. The findings below are mostly about the view layer, where a few seams don't hold up.

## 1. PR detail's checks depend on the PR being in the list cache — and fail into the exact misleading states the design tries to avoid

`PullRequestDetailView` (mobile/App/Views/PullRequestsView.swift:90) resolves `checksRef` by looking the PR up in `store.pullRequests`. Two failure modes:

- If the PR isn't in the list (list not yet loaded, refetched under a different state filter, or reached via deep link), `ref` is `nil`, `fetchChecks` sets `.loaded`, and the UI asserts **"No checks reported for this commit"** — precisely the false claim the `checksState` comment says it exists to prevent. The comment frames `nil` as "a non-GitHub source", but "PR missing from a shared list cache" is the more likely cause and it's indistinguishable here.
- If `store.selectedRepo` is `nil` when the one-shot `.task` fires, the guard returns, nothing retries, and `checksState` stays `.idle` — a permanent "Loading checks…" spinner.

The protocol already has `pullRequest(owner:repo:number:)`; the detail view should fetch its own PR when the list lookup misses (which also fixes the meta section silently vanishing). Alternatively, pass the `HGPullRequest` value into the view — which is exactly what the new `IssueDetailView` does. Having the two sibling detail views use opposite parameterization strategies (value-snapshot vs. number-plus-store-lookup) is the underlying incoherence; pick one, and the value-passing one eliminates this whole failure class.

## 2. `canHighlight` is dead API

`SyntaxHighlighter.canHighlight` (mobile/Sources/HyperGitCore/Syntax/SyntaxHighlighter.swift:76) has two overloads, extensive doc comments, and four tests — and no production caller. `FileViewerView` never consults it: for an oversized or unsupported file it still spins up the detached task, gets zero tokens, and silently shows plain text. Either wire it into `FileViewerView` to serve its stated purpose (skip the detached hop, and/or show a "highlighting skipped" note so the size cap is visible behavior rather than a silent degradation), or drop it. As shipped it's speculative surface area whose contract is enforced only by its own tests.

## 3. The shared `store.openFile` slot pushes race-handling into every consumer

The path-recheck dance in `loadAndHighlight` (mobile/App/Views/FileTreeView.swift:68) is correct, and the comment explaining it is honest — but that comment is describing a store design problem being patched at the call site. Every current and future consumer of `openFile` must independently rediscover and re-implement this guard. Having `store.loadFile` *return* the loaded file (or keying open files by path) would let the view own its data and delete both re-checks. Related gap while you're there: the guard compares only `file.path == path`, and `.task(id: path)` doesn't include `ref` — the same path viewed at two different refs will cross-talk (stale content passes the guard, and the task won't re-run on a ref change). The `id` predates this diff, but the new guard hardens the path dimension while leaving the ref dimension open; include `ref` in both.

## 4. Verify the detached highlight actually leaves the main actor

`FileViewerView` justifies its structure on highlighting running off the main thread, via `Task.detached` calling `SyntaxHighlighting.attributedString` (an App-target type). If the app target builds with default `@MainActor` isolation (the Xcode default for new Swift 6 targets), that call hops straight back to the main actor inside the detached task, silently defeating the design while keeping its complexity. Worth confirming, and cheap to make robust: mark `SyntaxHighlighting` (or the function) `nonisolated` so the intent is enforced by the compiler rather than by a build setting. Relatedly, `PatchView.render()` (mobile/App/Views/PullRequestsView.swift:307) does the equivalent work — split plus attributed-string build for up to 1000 lines — synchronously on the main actor on every expand. It's bounded so it's lower stakes, but the two views treat the same class of work inconsistently.

## 5. `checkRuns` interpolates `ref` unencoded while documenting branch/tag support

`GitHubClient.checkRuns` (mobile/Sources/HyperGitCore/Clients/GitHubClient.swift:111) builds the path with raw interpolation, and its doc comment invites "SHA, branch, or tag name" — but a branch like `feature/foo` breaks the path. Every in-repo caller only ever passes `checksRef` (a SHA), and `HGPullRequest.checksRef` deliberately guarantees that. Either narrow the doc to "commit SHA" so the contract matches actual safe usage, or percent-encode. As written, the API's documented surface is wider than its implementation supports, and the mismatch is exactly the kind a future caller trips on.

## 6. Minor design notes

- The default `checkRuns` implementation in the `RepositorySource` extension (mobile/Sources/HyperGitCore/Clients/RepositorySource.swift:20) means a source that *intends* to implement checks but mismatches the signature compiles silently against the no-op. It also makes "source has no concept of checks" indistinguishable from "fetch succeeded with zero runs" at the protocol level — acceptable here because `checksRef == nil` gates upstream, but worth knowing you have two independent gates encoding the same policy.
- `HGChecksSummary.label` puts user-facing display copy in the core model while `badgeColor` correctly lives in the app layer; the split is slightly inconsistent, though `label` is at least string-only.

## Missing tests

Core logic is well covered. The gaps are all at the seams identified above, and most would be closed structurally rather than by tests: nothing exercises the `checksRef`-nil → "No checks reported" path in finding 1 (hard to test as view code — another argument for moving the resolve-or-fetch decision into the store or a fetchable model), and the default `RepositorySource.checkRuns` extension is untested (one-line test if you keep it).
